[15:00] Samira Patel: hey everyone good afternoon thanks for joining, i'm Samira from Redwood inference — i'm the AE on this account. today's goal is to understand your p95 targets and concurrency so we can propose the right deployment and pilot. jonas from our SE team will dig into perf details.
[15:01] Carlos Rivas: thanks, Samira. quick intro — i'm Carlos, CTO at GreenLight. we build a real-time triage assistant that summarizes lab notes and streams suggestions live to the clinician ui. latency is critical — we need model tokens to start streaming within a tight p95.
[15:02] Maya Kapoor: hi, maya here — we've been running a mix of open models on GPUs in-house and sometimes via managed endpoints. cost is a concern but we can't sacrifice p95; our target is 250-300ms p95 for first-stream token on a 1-2k token prompt, with sustained throughput for bursts.
[15:03] Jonas Meier: okay thanks. to be explicit, is that 250-300ms p95 for the first token (TTFS) or for full response p95?
[15:03] Maya Kapoor: it's for the first token — clinicians need immediate streaming feedback. overall response can be longer but the initial token needs to be snappy.
[15:04] Ethan Cho: hi, ethan infra — we also care about concurrent sessions. baseline expected steady concurrency is ~150 simultaneous streaming sessions, peak bursts up to 900 for a few minutes during morning rounds.
[15:05] Samira Patel: that's super helpful. so rough numbers: 250-300ms TTFS p95, steady 150 conc, spikes to 900. do you have a cadence for those spikes (minutes/hours)?
[15:05] Ethan Cho: spikes are 5-10 minutes typically, sometimes 20. frequency daily during shift changes.
[15:06] Jonas Meier: okay, couple of follow-ups: what's your typical prompt length and response token budget? you mentioned 1-2k prompt — is that tokens or characters?
[15:06] Maya Kapoor: tokens. average prompt ~800 tokens, up to 2k. responses are usually 100-400 tokens. some cases run longer but rare.
[15:07] Samira Patel: got it. for that mix there are a few levers: hosted multi-tenant (fast onboarding), Dedicated reserved pools (predictable latency under burst), and Private (VPC/on-prem) for data residency. which deployment modes are you allowed to consider?
[15:07] Priya Shah: from security, we prefer dedicated or private — we need audit logs, KMS integration, and SSO/SAML. SOC2 compliance is mandatory.
[15:08] Samira Patel: we can support those. Redwood Dedicated offers KMS integrations and per-tenant audit logs; Private gives you the full VPC control. Hosted can get you to market fastest but requires data handling agreement.
[15:09] Carlos Rivas: cost is also a gating factor. what's the unit economics difference between Hosted and Dedicated for heavy streaming workloads? ballpark is fine.
[15:09] Jonas Meier: ballpark: for streaming-heavy workloads Dedicated reduces per-token cost via reserved capacity and better batching control. Hosted inclines to be higher per-token but lower ops overhead. with autoscaling and intelligent batching we can often match latency SLOs while saving cost, but it depends on your burst profile. given frequent sub-20-minute spikes to 900 conc, Dedicated gives better predictability.
[15:11] Maya Kapoor: do you have quantization profiles? we currently run 4-bit quantized models in-house to reduce GPU memory, but we've seen p95 regress in some cases.
[15:11] Jonas Meier: yes, Redwood Optimize will suggest quantization that is validated per-model. we support quantized variants and offer benchmarked perf profiles — sometimes 4-bit gives huge cost win with small quality loss, but on streaming p95 you'd want to validate. our standard approach: run model A/B on identical prompt sets and measure p95 TTFS and token/sec.
[15:12] Ethan Cho: what about caching? can prefix or KV cache help our 800-token prompts?
[15:12] Jonas Meier: yes, prefix and KV caching can significantly reduce compute for repeated context. if prompts share histories (e.g., patient summaries), caching KV can drop compute and improve p95 for subsequent tokens. for first-token of a novel prompt caching less helpful. also continuous batching helps throughput but may add micro-latency — tradeoffs to tune.
[15:13] Samira Patel: quick real example — a customer with similar behavior moved to Dedicated 2x GPUS per shard, used prefix caching and smart routing and saw p95 TTFS drop by ~30% in steady state and reduced cost by ~40% vs naive Hosted.
[15:14] Priya Shah: curious about fallback strategy — if Dedicated capacity is full during a spike can we fall back to Hosted automatically without exposing PHI?
[15:14] Jonas Meier: yes, Redwood supports policy-based routing. you can configure fallback tiers; for Private/ Dedicated we can restrict data residency. for fallbacks we can route to a dedicated burst pool or to a Hosted variant that strips or encrypts sensitive fields — depends on your compliance posture.
[15:15] Maya Kapoor: about benchmarking — what do you need from us to run a representative p95 and token/sec bench?
[15:15] Jonas Meier: ideal: 48-72 hours of request traces (timestamps, prompt lengths, response lengths, error codes), and two canonical prompt sets: one 'short-high-frequency' and one 'long-heavy-context'. we'll provide a test harness to replay at controlled conc and burst profiles.
[15:16] Carlos Rivas: we can export traces but will need guidance on redaction for PHI.
[15:16] Priya Shah: security note — any data we share must be encrypted in transit and at rest; we'll need a DPIA for the pilot.
[15:17] Samira Patel: absolutely — we'll share our data handling agreement and recommended redaction practices. Redwood's pilot contracts can include a limited DPIA and we support encrypted S3 for traces, plus KMS-managed keys.
[15:18] Jonas Meier: for the benchmark run we'll measure: TTFS p95/p99, sustained token/sec per GPU, tail latency under burst, and cold-start impact. cold-start here includes KV warmup.
[15:18] Maya Kapoor: can you also measure end-to-end client perceived latency? sometimes model side is fast but network adds 100-200ms.
[15:19] Jonas Meier: yes we'll instrument both server-side and client SDK latencies. recommend colocated probes (from your east coast and west coast clinics) to capture network variance.
[15:20] Ethan Cho: ops question — do you support autoscaling that respects p95 SLOs vs cost? we prefer policy to avoid chasing cost at the expense of latency.
[15:20] Samira Patel: Redwood Dedicated has autoscaling policies with SLO-aware thresholds — you can set target p95 and min/max capacity, with burst buffers. If policy detects risk to p95 it scales proactively (within limits) and can trigger fallback policies.
[15:22] Maya Kapoor: what about streaming throughput numbers — what's achievable token/sec per GPU for a model like the one we use (Llama2-70B-style architecture, quantized)?
[15:22] Jonas Meier: rough public ballpark: for a 70B-class model on optimized kernels with quantization and continuous batching you might see 150-600 tokens/sec per GPU depending on sequence lengths and attention optimizer. short tokens and heavy batching push upper end; streaming with low-latency target tends toward the lower half. we'll produce more specific numbers after we run your prompts.
[15:23] Carlos Rivas: if we need to get below 300ms p95 we may have to split model or use a smaller distilled variant for first-pass streaming and escalate for full answer — is hybrid pipeline supported?
[15:24] Jonas Meier: yes — Redwood supports multi-model routing. you can route initial streaming to a smaller low-latency model, then fan-out a second request to the larger model for full context when needed. that pattern helps surface first token quickly and improves p95.
[15:25] Priya Shah: any audits or docs you can share on encryption and logs?
[15:25] Samira Patel: i'll share our security pack (SOC2 Type II, encryption at rest/in transit, KMS integrations, RBAC docs) after the call. also we can sign an NDA if required.
[15:26] Maya Kapoor: latency under cold cache — how much does KV cache warmup affect the p95 during a spike?
[15:26] Jonas Meier: it depends on reuse. If the spike contains many unique prompts cold goes up. KV warmup cost is visible in the first few tokens. We usually measure cold-start delta and recommend a warm pool or pre-warming strategy for predictable shift changes.
[15:27] Ethan Cho: our infra team prefers Dedicated with burst pool and a policy to allow limited fallback to Hosted for stateless requests. can you map what that architecture would look like?
[15:27] Jonas Meier: sure — architecture sketch: Dedicated primary pool (reserved), a smaller dedicated burst pool (on demand), and Hosted fallback tier for non-PHI or masked requests. Smart router handles routing by policy and request annotation. We can produce a formal architecture doc.
[15:29] Carlos Rivas: timeline — we're hoping to run a pilot in february with engineering sign-off by end of march. is that feasible?
[15:29] Samira Patel: yes. proposed: collect traces by 1/23, bench run week of 1/26, pilot kickoff 2/9, 4-week pilot.
[15:30] Maya Kapoor: one last thing — how do you track quality regressions if we change quantization or model variants? we need guardrails.
[15:30] Jonas Meier: Redwood Optimize includes eval hooks and regression alerts tied to your prompt sets. we can run continuous A/B and measure rouge/accuracy/clinician acceptance metrics and raise alerts if regressions exceed thresholds.
[15:31] Priya Shah: ok thanks. security will review SOC2 pack and KMS options.
[15:32] Samira Patel: recap then actions — we will: share security docs and pricing, provide test harness and benchmark plan, and run the p95/token/sec bench once we have traces. we'll also propose Dedicated pool sizing and fallback policies.
[15:33] Carlos Rivas: perfect. thanks everyone.
[15:34] Samira Patel: thanks all — we'll follow up with the materials this week.
